extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, practicing chymists and physicians, and scholarly readers of early-modern chemical philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging claims about the elementary nature of substances (salt, sulphur, mercury) and the validity of chymical/anatomical experiments and nomenclature. Focuses on what counts as sufficient experimental proof, how naming should be justified, and which observed properties are diagnostically relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle must be perfectly homogeneous (true element/principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true Principle or Element must be "perfectly Homogeneous" and not a body that is "further Resoluble into any number of Distinct Substances"; if it is resoluble, it cannot be regarded as a primitive Element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists that elements/principles should not merely be predominant qualities in a mixt body but strictly simple and homogeneous. Products of chymical anatomy that can be further decomposed (e.g. into saline, unctuous, and other liquors) should be treated as compounded, not as genuine Elements. Example: challenge to calling a distill'd oil the true Sulphur until ocular proof of homogeneity is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental/ocular proof required for claims of elemental identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that a dissected product (from fire, distillation, or extraction) is a true Element must be supported by "ocular proof" or experimental demonstration rather than by analogy or loose nomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly demands that Chymists 'give us an ocular proof' that a given distillate is a homogeneous principle. Mere resemblance or predominancy of some qualities is insufficient. The burden is on practitioners to show by experiment that the supposed principle exists in the claimed pure form in the materia prima.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance in some qualities is insufficient evidence of identity
rubrics_metrics.description: A similarity in one or a few obvious qualities (e.g. inflammability, heat, dryness, or taste) does not prove two bodies are of the same nature or deserve the same name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit anti-patterns: equating flame with Elemental Fire because it is hot/dry; calling ashes 'Earth' because they resemble earth in some respects. The author warns that analogy/partial resemblance is 'more plausible than cogent' and must not substitute for demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not name substances from mere predominancy of a quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving a substance the name of the 'predominant principle' (salt, sulphur, mercury) because one quality predominates is not a justifiable practice without proof of simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes the Chymists' custom of bestowing names on distillates merely because a particular quality is conspicuous (e.g. 'salt' because it tastes). He calls this a license to 'abuse Words' and argues naming must follow demonstration of true elemental nature, not dominant sensorial traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple independent properties as diagnostic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish substances by a range of physical and chemical properties (taste, smell, inflammability, volatility/fixity, miscibility with water, fusibility, color, consistence, crystal form, coagulability, medicinal virtues) rather than a single trait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author lists many diagnostic qualities and gives experiments: volatile vs fixt salts (salt of tartar vs hartshorn); oils that float or sink; different crystal shapes of salts; differing medicinal effects (e.g. saline spirits of urine vs blood). He warns Chymists over-rely on a few properties (e.g. 'tast' or 'inflamability') to classify principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that preparation methods can produce new mixts (method-induced artifacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Products obtained by fire, distillation, or solvent extraction may be artefacts or new compounded bodies produced by the operation itself, not pre-existing elementary ingredients of the original matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly notes that 'productions of the Fire' or extracts by Spirit of Wine may be 'a new kind of Mixts' or a 'Magistery' and thus not antecedent principles. Examples: fixed salts from incineration, volatile salts from gentler distillation, spirit of wine dissolving resins to form compounds. Analysts must consider whether the operation created the observed product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency across sources required for a claimed universal principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If something is claimed to be a universal Principle (e.g. 'Sulphur' or 'Mercury'), it should be demonstrably the same homogeneous substance across different concretes (plants, animals, minerals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author demands demonstration that the supposed principle exists in the same simple form in the various bodies it is said to compose. He contests claims that because many distillates resemble one another, they therefore are the same principle; instead, chymists must show homogeneity across sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish volatile and fixed species and do not conflate them as identical Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and document differences among volatile vs fixed salts (and among volatile salts themselves); volatility/fixity and differing behaviors under heat and in solvents indicate distinct substances, not the same elemental salt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: salt of tartar (fixt) vs salt of hartshorn (volatile); salt of amber, urine, skull differ in properties and medicinal uses. The author cites Boyle's and Helmont's observations and gives an experiment showing three different salts from urine. Practitioners should not generalize from one salt-type to all salts as a single Element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims about medicinal virtues require empirical specificity, not assumed transference
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not uncritically ascribe the medicinal virtues of a concrete to the salts/tinctures obtained by calcination/extraction without empirical evidence linking the product to the claimed therapeutic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author disputes the common practice of ascribing the virtues of calcinated bodies to the salts produced by incineration. He provides examples of differing 'vertues' among alkalizate salts (wormwood, eyebright, guaiacum) and cautions that many salts lose or change medicinal properties in the process of preparation; thus medical claims must be supported by observation and experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and clear, repeatable operational descriptions as part of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations used to support claims should be reproducible and accompanied by clear operational details (how heat, distillation, or reagents were applied), since differing procedures yield different products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text includes explicit experimental recipes and outcomes (e.g. annealing retorts, sand furnace, changes of receiver, heating stages) to show how procedure affects products (different oils, empyreumatical spirits, crystal forms). The implication is that reproducible procedure and reporting are required for claims to be persuasive.
